title: Prefetch delays and memory-bandwidth interaction - brief
content:
Summary:

Quick notes from an exploratory run investigating interactions between prefetch timing, memory bandwidth usage, and downstream eviction/paging behavior in our KV cache. This is a lightweight field doc (working-level) rather than a full experiment write-up; next step is to convert to an instrumentation + benchmark PR.

Why this matters:
- We add aggressive prefetch to reduce request tail latency by warming KV pages early.
- But on high-concurrency tails, prefetch traffic can saturate PCIe/DRAM bandwidth and trigger more evictions / paging, increasing average token cost and hurting latency.
- We need a rule-of-thumb and simple mitigations (delay horizon, rate-limiter) before rolling prefetch more broadly.

Goals:
- Establish whether prefetch timing is causing measurable bandwidth spikes that correlate with eviction/paging events.
- Quantify a safe prefetch delay window that maximizes reuse (hits) without increasing eviction/paging.
- Produce actionable mitigations for the runtime (heuristics + quick flags).

Cluster & workload used:
- Cluster: 8x A100-80GB nodes (nvlink disabled), Linux 5.19, driver 530.xx
- Memory: 256GB host DRAM, 40GB GPU VRAM; KV store kept primarily on host with pinned pages + DMA to GPU when needed (our current deployment config)
- Workload: mixed chat + completion traces from prod-sampled 2025-01 (seq len 64 median, 512 95p), QPS ranged 200-3k across experiments, concurrency varied 1-32 streams per GPU
- Model: Llama-2-13B equivalent; KV residency: average 18% of model keys resident (simulated warmset distributions)

Instrumentation:
- Traces: per-request timestamps (prefetch enqueue, DMA start, DMA end, kv-lookup start/end, eviction hooks)
- Perf counters: DRAM bandwidth via pcm-memory, PCIe bandwidth via nvidia-smi accounting, page-fault & swap counters from kernel (minimally sampled)
- Runtime metrics: reuse_rate (fraction of prefetched pages subsequently accessed), eviction_rate (pages evicted / second), paging_events (major+minor), tail P99 latency for token generation

Experiment matrix (high level):
- Baseline: no prefetch (on-demand only)
- P0: immediate prefetch (enqueue on request enqueue)
- P10: 10ms prefetch delay after request enqueue
- P50: 50ms prefetch delay
- P100: 100ms prefetch delay
- PAdaptive: heuristic delay = max( (estimated_kv_index - current_pos) * base_token_ms, min_delay ) with lightweight bandwidth cap
- Each variation run at QPS: 200, 800, 2000; concurrency: 4, 16, 32; repeated 6x for statistical smoothing

Key numeric observations (aggregated median across repeats):
- Baseline (no prefetch): reuse_rate ~ 0.0 (expected), eviction_rate 42 pages/s, DRAM BW baseline 45 GB/s, token P99 86ms
- P0 (immediate): reuse_rate 0.46, eviction_rate 79 pages/s (↑88%), DRAM BW spike to 92 GB/s (instantaneous), paging_events increased modestly (minor faults ↑120%), token P99 102ms (worse despite higher reuse)
- P10 (10ms delay): reuse_rate 0.44, eviction_rate 61 pages/s (↑45% vs baseline), DRAM BW peaks 68 GB/s, token P99 88ms (neutral/slightly worse)
- P50: reuse_rate 0.41, eviction_rate 48 pages/s (~baseline), DRAM BW peaks 52 GB/s, token P99 83ms (slightly better than baseline)
- P100: reuse_rate 0.36, eviction_rate 39 pages/s (↓7% vs baseline), DRAM BW peaks 49 GB/s, token P99 85ms
- PAdaptive (with bandwidth cap at 70 GB/s): reuse_rate 0.42, eviction_rate 46 pages/s, DRAM BW bounded near cap, token P99 81ms (best overall)

Immediate takeaway:
- Aggressive immediate prefetch (P0) increases reuse but saturates memory bandwidth and pressure -> more evictions and higher tail latency. Reuse alone is not predictive of improved end-to-end latency.
- A modest delay (50ms) reduces harmful bandwidth spikes while retaining majority of reuse; produced slightly better latency than baseline in these traces.
- Adaptive approach that senses bandwidth and gates prefetch performed best in balance of reuse vs eviction/tail latency.

Hypothesis / root cause (concise):
- Prefetch traffic is bursty and synchronous across many concurrent requests. When multiple streams prefetch at the same time, the cumulative read throughput exceeds host DRAM -> bottleneck moves from latency to bandwidth -> eviction and paging mechanisms (kernel pressure + our cache reclaimers) start thrashing the resident set. Net effect: more page churn, less useful cache residency, and overall worse latency despite higher micro reuse.

Evidence supporting hypothesis:
- Correlation plots show DRAM BW spikes aligned with prefetch DMA completion windows for P0 runs.
- Eviction_rate tracks with momentary BW > ~75 GB/s threshold across nodes.
- When we added a random jitter (±10–30ms) to prefetch enqueue times in P0 run, BW spikes smoothed and eviction_rate dropped by ~30% with only 5% drop in reuse_rate.

Simple mitigations (low friction):
1) Add a soft prefetch delay default = 30–50ms for multi-stream workloads. This buys time for some requests to complete and reduces synchronous bursts.
2) Add jitter to prefetch enqueue (uniform in [0, jitter_ms]) where jitter_ms configurable by deployment tier.
3) Bandwidth-aware prefetch gate: sample recent DRAM BW and if above threshold, throttle/skip prefetch. Conservative default threshold = 70 GB/s (observed sweet spot on our test nodes).
4) Replace synchronous large-page DMA with staggered small-chunk DMA where practical to smooth peaks.
5) Provide runtime flag to disable prefetch per-route/tenant (for high-BW-sensitive customers).

Longer-term mitigations / research directions:
- Adaptive per-warmset-prefetch: compute warmset heat (probability of reuse) and prefer prefetch for hotter keys only. This trades some reuse to reduce bandwidth.
- Priority queues for DMA: give higher priority to prefetches that are on the critical path for active requests while demoting speculative background prefetches.
- Integrated bandwidth-aware eviction: when detecting BW pressure, proactively reduce prefetch aggressiveness and increase hold-time of resident pages (avoid premature eviction churn).
- Model-side KV placement hints: if certain keys are heavily reused across requests, hint to keep them resident at higher priority.

Quick notes on measurement caveats / gaps:
- Our test nodes are NVLink-disabled (relevant to host<->GPU bandwidth). Behavior might differ on NVLink clusters; need a comparative run.
- pcm-memory gives host DRAM aggregates; we don't yet have per-process breakdown for all noise sources. Need to tie process-level BW to prefetch traffic more precisely.
- Swap/major page-faults are rare in these experiments but minor faults increased; need kernel-level tracing if we decide to pursue low-level reclamation changes.
- The workload here was skewed to medium-length sequences; very long-context (>2k) requests could have different dynamics (larger KV working set).

Action items (next 2 sprints):
- [Avery] Open an RFC/PR to add prefetch jitter + soft-delay + bandwidth gate to runtime (small flag-based change) — target: feature branch by 2025-03-12. linked PR stub: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/789 (WIP).
- [Riley] Run comparative experiments on NVLink-enabled nodes (timeline: 1 week) and produce delta table.
- [Samira] Add per-process bandwidth sampling (perf + procfs) instrumentation to tie prefetch traffic to BW counters (timeline: 2 weeks).
- [Luca] Prototype adaptive prefetch policy that uses recent reuse history to prioritize keys (timeline: spike in sprint).

Notes to reviewers / questions:
- Does the group think the 50ms default delay is conservative enough? On our traces 50ms was optimal-ish, but other deployments with lower inter-request arrival may be fine with smaller delay.
- Should this be enabled by default for Dedicated and Private customers, or gated behind an opt-in feature flag? My inclination: default-on for multi-tenant hosted, opt-in for Dedicated until we have NVLink runs.

Appendix (raw sample numbers for one representative node at QPS=2000, concurrency=32):
- P0: total_prefetch_bytes 12.1 GB/s (instant), average DMA latency 6.2 ms, eviction_rate 105 p/s, DRAM BW peak 94 GB/s, token P99 120ms
- P50: total_prefetch_bytes 6.2 GB/s (instant), average DMA latency 5.8 ms, eviction_rate 52 p/s, DRAM BW peak 53 GB/s, token P99 88ms
- PAdaptive: total_prefetch_bytes 7.1 GB/s, DMA latency 6.0 ms, eviction_rate 48 p/s, DRAM BW peak ~70 GB/s, token P99 82ms

References & links used during runs:
- Slack thread: #serving-runtime: "prefetch-bw-thrashing" (2025-02-09)
- Linear ticket: RD-1342 (prefetch policy experiment)

End.
